content: 1. All children suspected of having tuberculosis (TB) should undergo diagnostic testing. This is a conditional recommendation, acknowledging resource implications and based on very low-quality evidence. 2. The Xpert MTB/RIF test may be used as a replacement for conventional diagnostic methods (such as microscopy, culture, or histopathology) when testing specific non-respiratory specimens, such as lymph nodes or other tissues, in children suspected of having extrapulmonary TB. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 3. For children suspected of having TB meningitis, Xpert MTB/RIF should be used as the initial diagnostic test in preference to conventional microscopy and culture when testing cerebrospinal fluid specimens. This is a strong recommendation due to the urgency of rapid diagnosis, despite very low-quality evidence. 4. Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) should not replace the tuberculin skin test (TST) in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing latent TB infection in children or for the diagnostic work-up of children suspected of TB disease, regardless of HIV status. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 5. Commercial serodiagnostic tests should not be used in children suspected of having active pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, regardless of their HIV status. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence regarding the use of commercial serodiagnostics. 6. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients, including children, with presumptive or diagnosed TB. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 7. For the treatment of TB in children, the following daily dosages of anti-TB medications are recommended: Isoniazid (H): 10 mg/kg (range 7–15 mg/kg), maximum dose 300 mg/day. Rifampicin (R): 15 mg/kg (range 10–20 mg/kg), maximum dose 600 mg/day. Pyrazinamide (Z): 35 mg/kg (range 30–40 mg/kg). Ethambutol (E): 20 mg/kg (range 15–25 mg/kg). This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 8. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis living in settings with low HIV prevalence and/or low isoniazid resistance, and who are HIV-negative, can be treated with a three-drug regimen (HRZ) for 2 months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 4 months, using the dosages specified above. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 9. Infants aged 0–3 months with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis should be promptly treated with standard treatment regimens. Dose adjustments may be required to account for age and potential toxicity in young infants, and such decisions should be made by a clinician experienced in managing pediatric TB. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 10. During the continuation phase of TB treatment, thrice-weekly regimens may be considered for children who are not HIV-infected and are living in settings with well-established directly observed therapy (DOT). This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence for intermittent treatment in specific settings. 11. Streptomycin should not be used as part of first-line treatment regimens for children with pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 12. Children with suspected or confirmed tuberculous meningitis or osteoarticular TB should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for 2 months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 10 months, for a total treatment duration of 12 months. The dosages recommended for tuberculous meningitis are the same as those for pulmonary TB. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 13. Children living with HIV who are older than 12 months of age, unlikely to have TB disease based on symptom-based screening, and without contact with a TB case should be offered 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention and care package if living in settings with high TB prevalence. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 14. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis living in settings with high HIV prevalence (or with confirmed HIV infection) should not be treated with intermittent regimens (e.g., twice-weekly or thrice-weekly doses). This is a strong recommendation based on low-to-moderate quality evidence against the use of intermittent treatment in children. 15. Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculous meningitis caused by multidrug-resistant bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone as part of an appropriate MDR-TB regimen within a well-functioning MDR-TB control program. The decision to treat should be made by a clinician experienced in managing pediatric TB. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 16. All individuals with active TB should receive an assessment of their nutritional status and appropriate counseling based on their nutritional status at diagnosis and throughout treatment. This is a strong recommendation, although the quality of evidence is not available. 17. School-age children, adolescents, and adults (including pregnant and lactating women) with active TB and severe acute malnutrition should be treated in accordance with WHO recommendations for managing severe acute malnutrition. Children under 5 years of age with active TB and severe acute malnutrition should also be managed according to WHO guidelines for this age group. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 18. School-age children, adolescents, and adults with active TB and moderate undernutrition who fail to regain normal body mass index after 2 months of TB treatment, or who lose weight during treatment, should be evaluated for adherence and comorbid conditions. They should also receive nutritional assessment and counseling and, if indicated, be provided with locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore normal nutritional status. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 19. Children under 5 years of age with active TB and moderate undernutrition should be managed like other children with moderate undernutrition, including the provision of locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore appropriate weight-for-height. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 20. In settings where contact tracing is implemented, household contacts of people with active TB should undergo nutritional screening and assessment as part of contact investigation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 21. All suspected malaria cases should undergo parasitological testing (microscopy or malaria rapid diagnostic test [RDT]) to confirm the diagnosis. Both microscopy and RDTs should be supported by a quality assurance program. This is a good practice statement. 22. Children and adults with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (except pregnant women in their first trimester) should be treated with one of the recommended artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs): artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, or artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. This is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. 23. ACT regimens should provide 3 days of treatment with an artemisinin derivative. For dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, the recommended dose is 5 mg/kg body weight (bw) of dihydroartemisinin and 20 mg/kg bw of piperaquine daily for 3 days. This is a strong recommendation based on pharmacokinetic modeling. 24. To reduce transmission of treated P. falciparum malaria, a single dose of 0.25 mg/kg bw primaquine should be added to ACT for patients (except pregnant women, infants under 6 months, and breastfeeding women with infants under 6 months). Testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is not required. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 25. Infants weighing less than 5 kg with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with ACT at the same mg/kg bw target dose as for children weighing 5 kg or more. This is a strong recommendation. 26. In people co-infected with HIV/AIDS and uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria, avoid artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine if they are being treated with co-trimoxazole, and avoid artesunate-amodiaquine if they are being treated with efavirenz or zidovudine. This is a good practice statement. 27. For severe malaria, treat adults and children (including infants, pregnant women in all trimesters, and lactating women) with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours and until they can tolerate oral medication. Once parenteral therapy is completed, treatment should be completed with 3 days of ACT (adding a single dose of primaquine in low-transmission areas). This is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. 28. If artesunate is not available, artemether is preferred over quinine for treating severe malaria in children and adults. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 29. For pre-referral treatment of severe malaria, where complete treatment is not possible but injections are available, administer a single intramuscular dose of artesunate and refer the patient to an appropriate facility. If intramuscular artesunate is unavailable, use intramuscular artemether or, if that is also unavailable, intramuscular quinine. For children under 6 years, a single rectal dose of artesunate (10 mg/kg bw) may be used if intramuscular injection is not available, followed by immediate referral. Rectal artesunate should not be used in older children or adults. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 30. Children with acute otitis media should be treated with oral amoxicillin at 40 mg/kg twice daily for 7–10 days. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 31. In settings where pathogens causing acute otitis media are known to be sensitive to co-trimoxazole, this antibiotic may be used as an alternative, given twice daily for 7–10 days. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 32. Children with chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) should receive aural toilet by dry wicking and instillation of quinolone-containing ear drops (e.g., ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, or ofloxacin) three times daily for two weeks. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 33. Children who fail to respond to treatment for CSOM should be referred for further evaluation to investigate other causes, particularly tuberculosis. This is a strong recommendation based on expert opinion. 34. Topical steroids should not be used in the treatment of CSOM. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 35. There are currently no GRC-approved recommendations for dengue. Guidance is being updated, but the 2009 guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, and control may be used in the interim. 36. Children with acute bacterial meningitis should be treated empirically with third-generation cephalosporins: Ceftriaxone: 50 mg/kg per dose IV every 12 hours or 100 mg/kg once daily. Cefotaxime: 50 mg/kg per dose every 6 hours for 10–14 days. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence.
